greek_priam.name: begets fifty sons and many daughters as the patriarch of the Dardanid house
greek_priam.notes: Iliad 24.495-497: Priam tells Achilles he had fifty sons, nineteen from one womb (Hecuba), the rest by other women of the palace; among them Hector, Paris, Deiphobus, Helenus, Cassandra, Polyxena and Troilus.

greek_priam.name: ransoms the body of Hector by supplicating Achilles in his own tent
greek_priam.notes: Guided by Hermes through the Achaean camp, the aged king clasps Achilles' knees and kisses the hands that killed his son, moving Achilles to pity and to release Hector's corpse (Iliad 24).

greek_polyxena.name: bares her throat to the sacrificial blade and dies as a free woman with heroic composure
greek_polyxena.notes: In Euripides' Hecuba the messenger Talthybius reports that Polyxena tore open her robe and offered her breast/throat to Neoptolemus, refusing to be held, and won the admiration of the watching army for her courage.

greek_proetus.name: fortifies Tiryns with massive Cyclopean walls built by the seven Cyclopes
greek_proetus.notes: Apollodorus and Pausanias: Proetus brought the Cyclopes (Gasterocheires), seven in number, from Lycia and they raised the great unhewn-stone walls of Tiryns.

greek_proetus.name: sends Bellerophon to Iobates bearing a sealed letter ordering his own death
greek_proetus.notes: After his wife Stheneboea (Anteia) falsely accused Bellerophon, Proetus, unwilling to kill a guest himself, dispatched him to Lycia carrying folded tablets with deadly tokens (the proverbial 'Bellerophontic letter').

greek_telemachus.name: comes of age under Athena's guidance, journeying to Pylos and Sparta to seek news of his father
greek_telemachus.notes: The opening four books of the Odyssey (the Telemachy) trace his passage to manhood: prompted by Athena (as Mentes/Mentor) he confronts the suitors and sails to Nestor at Pylos and Menelaus at Sparta.

greek_telemachus.name: fights at his returned father's side to slay the suitors in the hall
greek_telemachus.notes: In the mnesterophonia he arms, bars the doors, and stands with Odysseus, Eumaeus and Philoetius against Penelope's suitors.

greek_tyndareus.name: binds all of Helen's suitors by oath, sworn on a sacrificed horse, to defend her chosen husband
greek_tyndareus.notes: On Odysseus' advice Tyndareus made every suitor swear over the severed pieces of a sacrificial horse to uphold and avenge the marriage of whoever won Helen — the legal compact that later raised the Greek host for Troy.

greek_tithonus.name: lives on deathless but ever-aging, withering until only his voice remains
greek_tithonus.notes: Eos won him immortality from Zeus but forgot eternal youth; he shrank into helpless old age, his endless babble all that was left, and in later tradition dwindled into a cicada (tettix).

greek_thyestes.name: claims the throne of Mycenae by producing the golden-fleeced lamb, token of Pelopid kingship
greek_thyestes.notes: Through Aerope he obtained the chrysomallos lamb that conferred the kingship and used it to wrest rule from Atreus; the sun then reversed its course (rising in the west) as Zeus' sign confirming Atreus instead.

greek_thyestes.name: begets the avenger Aegisthus on his own daughter Pelopia per the oracle
greek_thyestes.notes: Told by an oracle that only a son got upon his daughter could avenge him, Thyestes lay with Pelopia in disguise; the child Aegisthus later killed Atreus and restored him.

greek_pierus.name: gives his name to Pieria, the Muse-haunted land at the foot of Olympus
greek_pierus.notes: Eponymous founder of the Pierian region sacred to the Muses; father of Hyacinthus by the Muse Clio in Apollodorus.

greek_xuthus.name: fathers Achaeus and Ion, eponymous ancestors of the Achaeans and Ionians
greek_xuthus.notes: Son of Hellen, he marries Creusa of Athens; his sons Achaeus and Ion give their names to two of the great Greek divisions (the Ionians through Ion, his adopted/Apolline son in Euripides).

guanche_achaman.name: creates and sets in order earth, sky, water, fire, air, mountains, plants and animals from chaos
guanche_achaman.notes: Espinosa and Abreu Galindo record Achamán as the eternal, omnipotent father from whom all things derive their being; he establishes cosmic order.

sources.reference: A. de Espinosa, Historia de Nuestra Señora de Candelaria (1594)

guanche_achuguayo.name: governs time and the seasons as the moon, the 'Father of Times'
guanche_achuguayo.notes: Moon-god of Tenerife styled the 'Father of Times' (Padre de los Tiempos); he was said to dwell in the heights and descend to hear the Guanches' prayers.

sources.reference: Bethencourt Alfonso, Historia del pueblo guanche

guanche_magec.name: is captured by Guayota and shut within Teide, plunging the world in darkness until Achamán frees him
guanche_magec.notes: The central Guanche solar myth: Guayota abducts Magec the sun into the volcano; the Guanches pray to Achamán, who defeats Guayota, releases Magec and seals the demon in Teide.

guanche_magec.name: the radiant disk of the sun he bears across the sky

guanche_acoran.name: the almogarén, the open-air high sanctuary where offerings rose to him (e.g. Roque Bentayga, Risco Caído)

guanche_chaxiraxi.name: the dark Marian image of Candelaria with which her cult was syncretized

guarani_jasy_jatere.name: the wild honey with which he lures and feeds the children he carries off

greek_thetis.name: the divine armour and shield she obtains from Hephaestus for Achilles

sources.reference: C. Nimuendajú, Die Sagen von der Erschaffung und Vernichtung der Welt als Grundlagen der Religion der Apapocúva-Guaraní (1914)

greek_priam.gloss: Priam (born Podarces, 'swift-foot', renamed when ransomed by Hesione)
godlike / illustrious (recurrent Homeric epithet of Priam)

greek_tityus.gloss: son of Gaia / earth-born (he was carried to term by the Earth)

greek_sarpedon_lycian.gloss: godlike (epithet of Sarpedon in the Iliad)

greek_telemachus.gloss: prudent / sound of understanding (recurrent Homeric epithet)

greek_tantalus.gloss: sons of Tantalus (the accursed Pelopid/Atreid line named for him)

guanche_achaman.gloss: the great, the sublime, the sustainer of heaven and earth (titles recorded for the high god)

guanche_chaxiraxi.gloss: she who sustains/holds the heavens and the earth (the Sun Mother)

guanche_achuguayo.gloss: Father of Times (rendering of his title as governor of time and seasons)

guarani_jasy_jatere.gloss: a little piece of the moon

greek_pollux.name: the Dioscuria, Spartan festival of the Twins
greek_pollux.notes: At Sparta the Dioscuri were honoured with sacrifices, feasting and drinking; the twin beams of the dokana embodied them and were carried to war by the Spartan kings. Invoked across the Greek world as Soteres ('Saviours') and Anakes ('Lords'), especially by sailors and soldiers.

greek_polyxena.name: sacrifice on the tomb of Achilles
greek_polyxena.notes: The shade of Achilles demanded her blood; Neoptolemus slew her as priest over his father's grave-mound to appease the hero and gain fair winds for the Greek return (a sphagia / hero-cult offering).

greek_telesphorus.name: the Telesphorion in the Asklepieion of Pergamon
greek_telesphorus.notes: Telesphorus had his own round shrine within the precinct of Asclepius at Pergamon and was worshipped as the third member of the healing triad (Asclepius, Hygieia, Telesphorus) presiding over recovery and convalescence; his cult spread widely in the Roman period.

greek_tenes.name: the precinct of Tenes on Tenedos
greek_tenes.notes: The Tenedians founded a sanctuary to their eponymous hero where sacrifices were offered; no flute-player might enter the precinct (because a flute-player bore false witness against him) and the name of Achilles, his slayer, could not be uttered within it.

greek_thetis.name: the Thetideion shrine in Thessaly
greek_thetis.notes: Thetis had a sanctuary (the Thetideion) between Old and New Pharsalus in Phthiotic Thessaly, her ancestral region, and was also honoured at Sparta and in Messenia.

greek_praxithea.name: first priestess of Athena Polias
greek_praxithea.notes: In Euripides' Erechtheus the goddess Athena, after Praxithea consents to her daughter's patriotic sacrifice, establishes Praxithea as the first priestess of Athena Polias on the Acropolis and ordains cult honours for the dead daughters as the Hyacinthides.

guanche_chaxiraxi.name: the harvest festival of the Sun Mother
guanche_chaxiraxi.notes: Chaxiraxi was honoured at a festival at the close of the harvest at which milk, gofio (flour of roasted grain) and the meat of sheep and goats were shared; the date and rite underlie the later 15 August feast of the Virgin of Candelaria.

guanche_acoran.name: offerings at the almogarén high places
guanche_acoran.notes: On Gran Canaria the faycan and guanartemes led pilgrimages, libations of milk and offerings of butter and grain at open-air sanctuaries (almogarén) on sacred rocks to secure rain, fertility and protection from Acorán.

guanche_magec.name: the Beñesmen new-year harvest festival
guanche_magec.cadence: annual (first new moon after the summer solstice / harvest)
guanche_magec.notes: Beñesmen ('the great heats'), the Guanche new year held after the harvest, fell in the season of the sun's strength associated with Magec and marked thanksgiving for the gathered crops.

attributes.name: depicted as a youthful horseman in a pilos cap crowned by a star
attributes.notes: The Dioscuri are shown as paired beardless riders wearing the conical pilos (the half of Leda's egg) surmounted by a gleaming star; their duality is marked by paired emblems — two amphorae, two shields, two snakes.

attributes.name: symbolized by the dokana, two upright timbers joined by crossbeams
attributes.notes: The aniconic dokana represented the Twins at Sparta and accompanied the kings on campaign.

sacredAnimals.name: the horse (the oldest and chief attribute of the divine horsemen)

attributes.name: shown as one of the three enthroned judges of the dead, sceptre in hand, beside Minos and Aeacus
attributes.notes: In underworld scenes Rhadamanthus appears as a grave, sceptred judge assigning the dead; Homer places him in the Elysian plain rather than among the punished.

attributes.name: shown standing in a pool beneath a fruit-tree, the water receding and the boughs lifting from his reach
attributes.notes: The canonical image of his torment (the source of 'tantalize'): chin-deep in water that drains when he stoops and overhung by fruit the wind sweeps away when he reaches; in some versions a stone hangs over his head.

attributes.name: shown as a vast giant pinned to the ground while two vultures tear at his liver
attributes.notes: In Tartarus he is stretched over nine pelethra (about nine acres) with two vultures (or an eagle) feeding eternally on his ever-renewing liver, punishment for assaulting Leto.

attributes.name: shown shifting into fire, water, lion and serpent in the grip of Peleus who holds fast
attributes.notes: A favourite vase and gem subject: the wrestling of Peleus and the Nereid Thetis, she metamorphosing through fire, beasts and water as he refuses to let go.

sacredAnimals.name: the dolphin and the creatures of the sea that bear her

attributes.name: shown as a small hooded boy or dwarf wholly wrapped in a cucullus (hooded cloak)
attributes.notes: His unmistakable mark is the all-covering hooded cape; he is rendered as a child or dwarf, sometimes holding a scroll, and in the Gallo-Roman west is assimilated to the Genius Cucullatus.

attributes.name: shown as a youth on horseback ambushed by Achilles at the fountain-house by the Thymbraean precinct of Apollo
attributes.notes: One of the most popular subjects of Archaic vase-painting (e.g. the François Vase): Achilles springs from cover at the fountain to cut down the boy, often with Polyxena present; his death (before he reached twenty) sealed Troy's fall.

attributes.name: manifest as a great black dog (baddamulos) dwelling within Teide
attributes.notes: Guayota was pictured as a huge black dog, lord of the fire of the volcano, the mountain itself called Echeyde ('hell') as his abode.

sacredAnimals.name: the tibicenas, demon black dogs he commands

attributes.name: associated with the bright southern star Canopus
attributes.notes: As Sun Mother she was linked to Canopus, second-brightest star, visible low on the Canarian horizon.

attributes.name: a fanged, sheep-bodied wolf-headed beast that hunts in packs, named for its cry 'ao ao'
attributes.notes: Sixth of the seven monstrous sons of Tau and Keraná; only a climber up a tall pindó palm escapes it, since it can fell any other tree it circles.

sacredPlants.name: the pindó palm (the one tree it cannot fell, the refuge of its prey)

attributes.name: a small fair child with long blond hair (sometimes blue eyes), bearing a golden staff
attributes.notes: Alone among the seven brothers he is beautiful, not monstrous; lord of the siesta, he wanders at midday with a golden wand and a luring whistle to entrance children who do not nap.

sacredPlants.name: the yerba mate plant, of which he is protector
